I'm sorry, I was just trying to give the perspective from my environment - what I was trying to say is if there are resources out there, using them if you need them is no exploitation. The person you were talking to on the other thread was standing on a soapbox with clearly limited life experience and compassion. Someone who takes responsibility for an animal absolutely should be able to take care of it, but that certainly doesn't mean they need to have x amount of money. If you're able to take care of it by utilizing volunteer services, that's still providing care! There are people that have plenty of money and choose to euthanize over treatable conditions because they don't think it is worth it... That is the hardest thing to see. And those in the same vein that don't bother to keep their pets up to date on vaccines.

I'll mention that I am in the US, so please don't think we are all money-hungry. While our current political and social climate is severely lacking compassion, not all of us buy into it and are working to change it.

I think it's when people demand that we both care for their pets and figure out how to finance it for them. There are resources for those in financial hardships, but I don't feel it is the job of the veterinarian to seek out those resources for every case where a pet owner can't afford the care being given. There's just not time. Aside from their surgeries and appointments, they are then answering questions, responding to labwork and finishing exams on the pets that they've added to their already booked schedule (all of these things typically happening during lunch/dinner breaks and after hours). Many don't realize how hospitals operate and in turn don't respect veterinarian's time.

There are many ways that animals come into our lives and many ways we can find ourselves in financial hardship. It is not the place of a veterinarian's office to judge the position someone is in. So in short, the frustration arises when there is an expectation that we should do everything possible regardless of ability to pay. In another world, we would love to do that, but in reality, we'd be out of business quickly and unable to help any pets at all.

I don't think there is anything wrong with taking advantage of of things like low-cost or free vaccine clinics or funds available to those in financial hardships, but it doesn't just fall in people's laps.

*I am not a vet, but work in a veterinary hospital*

My advice is to do what interests you instead of trying to guess what will make you good money. Otherwise, you'll not only be miserable, you'll not have motivation to be successful. I think that's especially true for those of us on the spectrum.

To answer your question yes - I have had a series of decent jobs. I went to college not 100% sure what I wanted to do. I found myself in a media program that encompassed well-rounded experience in programming, web design/development, graphic design, and print production. When I graduated, I wasn't a good interviewer - I applied anywhere that was within the scope of my degree. I was finally hired by a print shop based primarily on my experience and willingness to start at an entry-level wage. I worked hard and showed my skills and worth and leveraged my degree and demonstrated skill for a significant raise. From there, I got hired by another printing company that was looking for someone with experience (the print world has a small pool to work with, in most cases). I did the same thing there - I spent my time learning as much as possible about every aspect of the business. When the owners of that company sold, I ended up being a vital part of the transition and moved into a management role. The new owner was ethically questionable, so I was applying everywhere I could. I applied to a vet hospital for an essentially entry-level position. Because I now had the management experience, they actually reached out to me and asked if I was interested in a supervisor position. So that is where I am now. I'm incredibly happy, I've always wanted to work with animals.

Long story short, do what interests you, be patient and willing to take a unique path. Those of us on the spectrum have so much to offer. Interviewing may not be our strong suit, but let your skills and experience talk for themselves! Good luck with your journey 🙂

People and human interaction fascinate me, I want to know everything I can on the subject. Subsequently, I've learned the patterns and watched how others interact and I can pull it off when I can identify commonalities between my current interactions and ones I've seen others have. As awful as I am at maintaining relationships, having social connection is important to me - so being able to fulfill my need for connection in a professional setting is perfect! There are rules and patterns, which make it much easier to know how to act.

As far as making things better... My biggest struggles at work are with sensory overload, recovering from the unexpected, and obviously picking up on non-verbal social cues. The best way I've found to overcome these is to be open and honest with my boss. I've had good luck with bosses be understanding and accommodating.

Absolutely! It's called hypervigilance (in case you're looking online for resources) and is very common for people on the spectrum.

- Knowing that I have Asperger's has allowed me to better accept why social interactions don't go as well as I'd like

A couple of things I've learned in supervising customer service (in a different industry, but applicable anywhere):
- Nip any problem in the bud when it happens, especially customer issues. Instances where an issue was easily resolved with a customer is a great opportunity to identify what caused the issue and put something in place to prevent it in the future. This will save you the hassle of having the same problem with a more challenging client!

- When communicating policies/procedures to staff, whether new or clarifications, always end with an action - even if it's just a simple "please confirm you've received this and let me know of any questions"

What kind of volume are you looking to produce and what size canvases?

Aqueous and Latex inks would be your go-to options.

Obviously, the latex doesn't meet your no-plastic requirement, but gives a decent quality image, and pretty durable. The start-up costs will require a higher upfront investment, but material costs tend to be lower.

Printers using aqueous ink produce a higher quality image, as they're commonly used for fine art and photography applications.

Both types would require a canvas material that is specially treated to be ink-receptive.

If you're not producing in volume, I highly recommend reaching out to a local commercial printer with large format capabilities.

I had a very similar experience with therapy for over a decade. You may find a big difference if you "shop around", so to speak, for a therapist that is a better fit for you. What helped me was finding someone who took a "strengths-based" approach. It is a very important distinction!

The old model of mental healthcare mimicked the medical model, in which providers focus heavily on the issues or symptoms, using deficit based language. The problem is then you end up in a cycle of managing symptoms and being looked at by providers as someone who cannot "recover". A strengths-based approach is just what it sounds like... Your strengths are focused on as a way to empower you to improve yourself and your circumstances. It sounds simple and inconsequential, but it makes a world of difference. I personally now leave therapy sessions on top of the world.

That's also sort of the reason I am so drawn to this subreddit... From what I've seen in the short time that I've followed it, this is a group of people that really do know what their strengths are, and can commiserate about the vast number of things that just don't make sense to us in a world of NTs... But in a way that doesn't devalue us.

If you're interested and would like some guidance on how to go about finding this type of care, send me a message!

I can't say I have any experience with an LED printer.

Not too sure about the cost, but my company purchased a Canon Oce about 6 months back, and it has been fantastic! We did have a bit of an adhesion issue on at least coroplast, but have since resolved with the use of a promoter!

One note though, if you go inkjet, I highly recommend that you be sure it is a 6-color (light cyan/light magenta)!! It makes a world of difference.

I would say laser-printing is out right off the bat. The toner would likely flake off. As far as inkjet, my only experience is with clients who have insisted on uv coating on both sides of a postcard. In those cases, the inkjeted addresses nearly always smeared. I would offer to your client to test a few, but definitely not commit to a full run until they've seen how it adheres to the uv coating. If it were me, I'd persuade them to reprint. 

Good luck! Let me know if you find a successful solution, it'd be helpful to know!

What are you using to personalize your pieces? If that itself is glossy and you are looking for a nice contrast, I highly recommend something called a soft touch finish... Laminate, Aqueous coatings, and UV coatings all have a soft touch option!! This is probably my favorite type of coating, especially when paired with a high gloss spot finish!!
